newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU edges towards BSE beef aid package.
newsitem.headline: EU edges towards BSE beef aid package.

text.p: European Union farm ministers edged towards agreement on Wednesday on a package of measures to provide extra aid for farmers hurt by the mad cow crisis and to cut beef surpluses.

EU officials said ministers, heading into the third day of their meeting, generally welcomed a new Irish EU Presidency text calling for an extra 500 milllion Ecus aid to break a deadlock with the European Commission over compensation for beef farmers.
"There is the basis for a deal," said Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely.
But he warned that there was no new money available in the 1997 EU budget and that member states might find it difficult to agree on how the aid should be shared.
The crisis was triggered by a British government statement in March that the fatal cattle brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to people.
EU beef demand has since fallen 15 percent and some 400,000 tonnes of unwanted beef has been taken into public stores.
EU farm ministers unanimously rejected an initial Irish compromise on Tuesday, saying aid was insufficient and measures to cut beef surpluses unacceptable.

France, which had been the most critical, softened its stance on Wednesday, with a French official saying the new text was "negotiable." Germany, which had also been highly critical, suggested that agreement could be reached on a smaller package, leaving out some of the longer term structural changes.
One of the main problems is a proposal for a 42 percent reduction in the number of German male cattle eligible for EU aid, a German official said.
It also wants the distribution of aid to be clarified.
The Irish presidency urged the Commission to make proposals urgently for further aid to farmers hit by the BSE crisis.

"The (Farm) Council considers that the continuing serious difficulties justify additional measures (including promotion) for the beef sector amounting to not less than 500 million Ecus," the presidency said in the new compromise paper.

It noted that 230 million Ecus of aid payable to beef producers in 1997 was brought forward to 1996 under an agreement drafted by EU farm ministers at an informal meeting in Killarney, Ireland, in September.
Commission officials noted that 270 million Ecus of savings still had to be found in the 1997 budget.

The EU's executive Commission previously argued that emergency aid agreed by EU leaders in Florence in June, topped up by national payments, would cover the livestock producers' estimated 1.2 billion Ecus losses in 1996.

Regarding aid in 1997 and 1998, Ireland has suggested that 60 percent of an estimated 1.3 billion Ecus aid due to oilseed farmers in 1997 be postponed until 1998, freeing more aid for livestock farmers.
Commission plans to slash payments to cash-rich cereal farmers to help pay for the beef package would be delayed until at least 1998 after opposition from nearly all member states.

An unpopular "Herod premium" for slaughtering new-born calves would be made optional with countries being able to choose instead a more expensive German scheme to encourage farmers to sell cattle earlier.
An Irish official said farm ministers were due to resume discussions at 1400 GMT after further changes to the compromise.
